setupSteps: Size the rope. Stand on the middle of the rope with one foot. Pull both handles straight up along your body. For a beginner the handle tops should reach about your armpits. Too long: the handles are above your shoulders, or the rope slaps the floor in a big loop; too short: the handles do not reach the chest and the rope feels tight. For a shorter rope choose a knot or trim the cord; a beaded or slightly heavier rope is easier to control for beginners (vendor advice, est.).

Choose the floor. Best: a sprung wooden floor or a thick rubber mat or exercise mat that does not slide. Avoid bare concrete, marble and tile, wet floors, loose rugs and carpet (the rope catches or bounces off). Shoes: supportive trainers with some cushioning (est.), not flip-flops, sandals or bare feet on tile; bare feet on a firm mat only if you are used to it.

Neighbour rule. If there are neighbours below, use the mat, keep jumps tiny (a centimetre or two of lift, a quiet rope such as a beaded or PVC one), skip in the daytime (not early morning or late at night over a bedroom, est.), and choose shadow skipping if the thud is a problem. Do not skip on a balcony slab or a floor you know carries sound.
Clear the room. About 2 m x 2 m of floor, 2.4 m ceiling (est.), no furniture, switched-off ceiling fan, no lights or hanging items above, no pets or children nearby.

Hand and arm position. Hold the handles lightly with the thumb along the handle. Hands about a hand's width away from the hips and a little in front, elbows bent about 90 degrees and tucked close to the ribs, forearms roughly parallel to the floor (est.).
Rope start position (basic bounce). Stand with the rope resting on the floor behind your heels. Swing it over your head as you hop.
Feet and stance. Feet together (basic bounce) or hip-width (alternate step), knees soft, standing tall, eyes forward at the horizon, not looking down at the feet.

Camera. Phone in landscape at about hip height (80-100 cm, est.), about 2.5 m in front for the feet and hands (front view), or at your side for knee bend and landing (side view). The whole body from the head to the floor is visible.
Clothing. Fitted sports clothes, a sports bra if needed, no loose dupattas or long kurtas that catch the rope, tie long hair back.
Warm up for 3-5 minutes (est.): march on the spot, ankle circles, heel raises, 10 calf raises, 5 easy bodyweight squats (Home 1), a few arm circles, then 10 shadow hops with no rope.

steps.title: Stand tall with the rope behind you
steps.action: Feet together, rope on the floor behind your heels, handles in each hand at hip height.
steps.feel: Even weight on both feet, calm and balanced.
steps.visualCheck: Side: ear, shoulder, hip and ankle roughly in one line, eyes forward. Front: shoulders level, elbows close to the ribs.

steps.title: Set the elbows and wrists
steps.action: Bend the elbows to about 90 degrees, tuck them in, and point the handles slightly out to the sides so the rope loops wide of the feet.
steps.feel: Shoulders relaxed, forearms level, wrists ready.
steps.visualCheck: Front: hands about a hand's width from the hips; handles not above the waist.

steps.title: Swing the rope over your head, without jumping
steps.action: Turn the wrists to swing the rope forward over your head and let it land in front of your toes. Stop it with your feet still on the floor.
steps.feel: Only wrists and forearms move; shoulders and arms stay quiet.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as the rope lands.
steps.visualCheck: Front: rope loop clears the head; hands move in small circles, not big arm swings.

steps.title: Practise the hop without the rope
steps.action: Do 5 tiny hops with the knees slightly bent, a centimetre or two off the floor, landing on the balls of the feet with heels barely touching.
steps.feel: Springy calves, soft knees, quiet landing.
steps.breathing: Breathe out as you land, in as you lift.
steps.visualCheck: Side: knees bend slightly on landing, back stays upright. Front: knees point over the toes, not caving in.

steps.title: Add the rope: one hop per turn
steps.action: Swing the rope over, and hop as it passes under the feet, just enough to clear it. Land softly on the balls of the feet.
steps.feel: Calves springing, wrists turning, rhythm steady.
steps.breathing: Breathe naturally; do not hold the breath.
steps.visualCheck: Side: feet lift about 2-3 cm (est.); back tall; eyes forward. Front: elbows steady at the sides.

steps.title: Stop and reset
steps.action: After 30 seconds (or when the rope tangles), stop, take a breath, set the rope behind you again.
steps.feel: Breathing a bit faster, legs warm.

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Start with the basic bounce rhythm. Get comfortable with 2-3 minutes in total of single bounces first (coaching guides, est.)

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Shift weight to one foot. On one rope turn, land on the left foot and lift the right foot just off the floor by a few centimetres

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Swap on the next turn. Land on the right foot, left foot lifts. Do not lift the knee high; the lift is small at first

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Build up in steps. Try three bounces, then one alternate step, then more alternates until all turns alternate (a common progression in coaching guides, est.)

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Keep it light. Land on the balls of the feet, knees soft, wrists turning, elbows tucked, arms still, eyes forward

steps.part: B. Alternate-foot step (jog step, running step)
steps.title: Rest 30 s between rounds, one calm breath at a time

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Stand tall, feet together, elbows bent at about 90 degrees, hands as if holding a rope

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Turn small circles with the wrists as if swinging a rope, hands a hand's width from the hips

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Hop lightly on the balls of the feet in time with the circles; keep the hops tiny and the heels barely touching the floor

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Alternate version: shift weight from left to right with each wrist circle (the quietest version in one source), landing softly

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Mat and shoes. Do it on a mat in trainers or on a sprung floor; if the thud is still too loud, go to marching on the spot with the same wrist circles

steps.part: C. Shadow skipping (no rope; quiet and low ceiling friendly)
steps.title: Shadow skipping gives less timing feedback than a real rope, so use it to learn the rhythm and for quiet days, not as a replacement for a rope when you want rope-specific speed training

commonMistakes.title: Jumping too high
commonMistakes.text: Jumping too high. Why: higher jumps mean harder landings, more tiredness and a louder thud for the flat below; one guide says you should not clear more than about an inch (2.5 cm) or so. Fix: hop just enough to clear the rope, 2-3 cm, "tiny and quiet".

commonMistakes.title: Landing flat or on the heels, or with locked knees
commonMistakes.text: Landing flat or on the heels, or with locked knees. Why: the shock goes up the shin, knee and back instead of being absorbed by the calf and knee. Fix: land on the balls of the feet with knees slightly bent; a few small hops without the rope first.

commonMistakes.title: Swinging the rope with big arm circles
commonMistakes.text: Swinging the rope with big arm circles. Why: wastes energy, tires the shoulders and makes the rope uneven. Fix: elbows tucked at your sides, hands close to the hips, wrists do the turning (coaching guides).

commonMistakes.title: Looking down at the feet
commonMistakes.text: Looking down at the feet. Why: rounds the upper back, breaks posture and loses timing. Fix: eyes on the horizon, a mark on the wall at eye level.

commonMistakes.title: A rope that is too long or too short
commonMistakes.text: A rope that is too long or too short. Why: too long: the rope catches or hits the floor in a loop; too short: the arms tense and the rope clips the head. Fix: step on the middle, handles to the armpits for a beginner; trim or knot to adjust.

commonMistakes.title: Skipping on a hard or uneven surface
commonMistakes.text: Skipping on a hard or uneven surface. Why: concrete and tile are the harshest for the shins, knees and feet; rugs catch the rope. Fix: a thick mat or sprung wooden floor; move to shadow skipping if only hard floors are available.

commonMistakes.title: Doing too much too soon (calf, shin, Achilles)
commonMistakes.text: Doing too much too soon (calf, shin, Achilles). Why: the calf and Achilles tendon take a lot of repeated load; shin splints and Achilles pain are among the common injuries listed by jump-rope coaches (commercial sources, not clinical trials). Fix: 30 s on / 30 s off for 6-8 rounds, add only one thing at a time, alternate with non-impact cardio, warm up the calves and stretch them after.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: raises blood pressure and brings dizziness (breathing study PubMed 7741618, carried from earlier items). Fix: breathe out on landing, in on lift.

commonMistakes.title: Wearing loose clothes, bare feet on tile or unsupportive shoes
commonMistakes.text: Wearing loose clothes, bare feet on tile or unsupportive shoes. Why: the rope catches, feet slip, no cushioning. Fix: fitted clothing, supportive trainers, a non-slip mat.

commonMistakes.title: Skipping through pain
commonMistakes.text: Skipping through pain. Why: pain in the shin, Achilles, knee or foot that builds up needs rest, not more reps (one source advises stopping rope work temporarily if Achilles symptoms start). Fix: stop, rest, switch to low-impact cardio and see a clinician if it lasts.

safetyNotes: Calf, Achilles and shin problems: coaches list Achilles tendon pain and shin splints among the common rope injuries; the advice is a warm-up, gradual progression, calf stretching and alternating with other cardio, and stopping temporarily if symptoms start (commercial sources, not clinical trials). Land on the balls of the feet with soft knees, use a mat, and do not skip two days in a row at the start.

Knee, hip, ankle, foot problems: the repeated landing can aggravate them; start with shadow skipping or marching, use a mat, keep hops at 2-3 cm, and stop with sharp or increasing pain. Some sources say mild osteoarthritis often tolerates controlled impact, but they stress individual assessment; I found no formal guideline (Not found).
Lower back pain: impact-related discomfort is a named issue in one hospital library; use shadow skipping or marching, small hops, and stop if the pain spreads down a leg.

High blood pressure and heart disease: skipping is a vigorous activity; get medical clearance first (University of Maryland medical system advice, snippet); breathe out on the effort; rope-specific blood pressure guidance: Not found.

Pregnancy and postpartum: impact can load the pelvic floor and may raise the risk of leaking or prolapse; stop or modify with any pain, leaking or pelvic heaviness; ask your obstetrician or a women's health physiotherapist; one source advises avoiding jumping until you can cough and sneeze without leaking. ACOG's own wording: Not found.

Osteoporosis: one expert quoted in a news article would not advise unsupervised jumping for someone with osteoporosis because of injury risk; people with a fragility fracture or low bone density should be assessed first.
Obesity: impact load on the joints can be substantial early on (hospital source); start with marching or shadow skipping and build up.
Floor and neighbours (Mumbai flat): use a thick non-slip mat, tiny hops, daytime only, and switch to shadow skipping if neighbours complain; never skip on a balcony slab or wet floor.
